title: Break-even analysis with a worked calculation for Strata and common-area cleaning
audience: Any strata and common-area cleaning operator who sets prices or plans monthly revenue, including solo operators with a small number of building contracts.
learningOutcomes: Classify the costs of a strata cleaning business as fixed or variable
Calculate monthly break-even revenue from fixed costs and a variable cost percentage
Explain why conflicting break-even figures must be reconciled before any of them is used

instruction.heading: What break-even means
instruction.body: Break-even revenue is the amount of sales that covers all costs exactly, so profit is zero. Below that level the business loses money. Above it, each further dollar of sales adds to profit. Strata work is mostly recurring, so for a common-area cleaner the figure tells you how many building contracts the business must hold each month before it covers its costs. It is a planning tool, and its answer is only as good as the costs and percentages behind it.

instruction.heading: Split costs into fixed and variable
instruction.body: Fixed costs do not change with the number of visits in a month. They include insurance, the vehicle, phone and software subscriptions, storage space and loan repayments. Variable costs move with each visit. They include consumables and chemicals used in a building, subcontracted crew hours and the card fees charged on each payment. Express variable cost as a percentage of sales: divide the variable cost in a period by the sales in the same period. ANZ defines the two cost types and warns that costs must be covered to avoid running at a loss (ANZ, 21 February 2025, last modified 22 July 2025). Check that percentage across at least three periods before relying on it.

instruction.heading: The formula
instruction.body: Break-even revenue equals fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage. The quantity one minus the variable percentage is the contribution margin: the share of each dollar of sales that is left to cover fixed costs. Use the variable percentage as a decimal, so 15 per cent becomes 0.15. The contribution margin of a 15 per cent variable cost is 0.85.

instruction.heading: Work the calculation in order
instruction.body: Write the inputs first, each with its source and date. Then compute the contribution margin. Then divide the fixed costs by it. Finally convert the result into a number of contracts at your average monthly contract value, and round up to whole contracts, because a part contract does not cover costs on its own. Xero's glossary gives a job count of 2.5 rounded up to 3 in practice (Xero Australia, 23 July 2026). Its example figures are for other businesses and are not used here.

instruction.heading: Reconcile before you use any figure
instruction.body: When two figures disagree, go back to the inputs. Confirm that each monthly contract value is a monthly amount and covers the stated number of visits, and not a per-visit price. Confirm that the variable percentage is a share of sales and not of cost. The vendor's common-area range of $1.80 to $3.00 per square metre per clean and its mid-rise range of $800 to $2,500 a month cannot be combined without knowing the area, the frequency and the scope behind each one (Clean Group, updated 15 March 2026). Reconcile them against one building before either goes into a plan or a quote.

procedure: List every monthly cost and label each one fixed or variable.
Work out variable cost as a percentage of sales for the same period, and check it across at least three months.
Calculate one minus the variable percentage to find the contribution margin.
Divide monthly fixed costs by the contribution margin to get break-even revenue.
Divide break-even revenue by your average monthly contract value to get the number of contracts needed, rounded up.
Compare any other break-even figure with your result, reconcile the inputs, and keep only the reconciled figure.

workedExamples.situation: A two-person strata cleaning business (illustrative figures, not market data) has fixed costs of $3,000 a month for insurance, the vehicle, software and storage, variable costs of 15 per cent of sales for consumables, card fees and subcontracted hours, and an average monthly contract value of $1,200 for a weekly common-area clean (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How many building contracts must the business hold each month to break even, and what should it reconcile before quoting?
workedExamples.reasoning: The contribution margin is 1 minus 0.15, which is 0.85. Break-even revenue is $3,000 divided by 0.85, which is $3,529.41 a month. Each contract contributes $1,020 ($1,200 multiplied by 0.85) towards fixed costs. That is 2.94 contracts, so the business needs 3 contracts. Before quoting, check that the 15 per cent includes every per-visit cost, that the $1,200 is a monthly figure for four weekly visits, and that the building's area and scope match the basis of any vendor figure. The vendor's mid-rise range of $800 to $2,500 a month sits around this figure, but its per-square-metre range does not reconcile with it (Clean Group, updated 15 March 2026).

equipmentAndPpe: Cost list for the last three months

commonErrors.prevention: Convert every cost to the same period before dividing, and label each input with its period.

commonErrors.error: Using variable cost as a share of cost instead of a share of sales
commonErrors.prevention: Divide variable cost by sales for the same period, and write the denominator beside the percentage.

commonErrors.error: Copying a break-even figure from a plan or a vendor guide without its inputs
commonErrors.prevention: Recalculate from your own inputs and record the source and date of each input before using the result.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Business planning only. This lesson gives no tax or accounting advice. Check the tax treatment of costs, and GST on your prices, with a registered tax agent or qualified accountant. The ATO's page on GST registration sets a $75,000 GST turnover threshold (last updated 14 September 2026).
This lesson does not grant any licence, registration or authority.

qualityStandard: Every break-even figure shows its fixed costs, variable percentage, period and source.
Two figures that disagree are reconciled before either one is used in a plan or a price.
documentationEvidence: Cost list split into fixed and variable, with source and date
Reconciliation note wherever two figures disagree
summary: Break-even revenue is fixed costs divided by one minus the variable cost percentage.
Use one period throughout the calculation.
Recalculate from your own inputs. Do not copy another plan's or a vendor's break-even figure.

knowledgeChecks.question: Break-even revenue is calculated as:
options: Fixed costs divided by (1 minus the variable cost percentage)
Fixed costs multiplied by the variable cost percentage
Sales minus fixed costs, shown as a percentage of the cost

knowledgeChecks.question: Fixed costs are $3,000 a month and variable costs are 15% of sales. What is the monthly break-even revenue?
Two sources give different break-even figures for the same building portfolio. What is the right response?
options: Use the larger figure to be safe and ignore the smaller figure entirely
Recalculate from your own costs and check each source's inputs before using any figure
Average the two figures together and quote the result to the committee today
Use the price list alone and skip the break-even check and rely on the owner's gut feel
